newsitem.title: UK: Princess Diana avoids embarrassing tribunal hearing.
newsitem.headline: Princess Diana avoids embarrassing tribunal hearing.

text.p: Princess Diana on Wednesday avoided an unprecedented appearance in a British court by agreeing to pay off a maid who claimed she had been wrongfully dismissed from the royal palace.
Frantic last-minute negotiations between lawyers for Diana and maid Sylvia McDermott, resulted in a settlement minutes before the start of an industrial tribunal hearing in London.
If the public hearing had gone ahead, Diana faced being called to appear as a witness over the dismissal of McDermott, who left Kensington Palace last September after nine years' employment.
But David Pannick, representing the princess who was cited by name in the official tribunal papers, told the hearing that the two parties had agreed a financial settlement.
"We are happy to tell the tribunal that the parties have reached agreement...The applicant (McDermott) has agreed that the sum of compensation should remain confidential," Pannick said.
McDermott, 44, who had earlier claimed she was dismissed without warning, said afterwards she was very pleased with the outcome of the case.
She declined to reveal how much she had won but told reporters "I am very satisfied...It is like winning the lottery. It's better than winning the lottery."
A spokeswoman for Diana said the princess was "delighted" with the settlement, adding "It vindicates the position she has adopted all along."
As part of the settlement, McDermott agreed to be bound by a confidentiality clause in the contract signed by all staff working in Britain's royal households.
She also agreed that she had been made redundant from the 9,000 pounds ($14,500) a year position, which came with an apartment at Diana's Kensington Palace.
The tribunal case attracted huge media attention in Britain, where life behind closed doors at Princess Diana's household is the subject of much intrigue and speculation.
A full hearing would have exposed the princess's private life to intense scrutiny and raised the undignified prospect of Diana being cross-examined as a witness.
McDermott is the latest in a string of Diana's retinue of cooks, nannies, driver and PR consultants to have departed from Kensington Palace.

The most dramatic resignations have come in the past 18 months when her press secretary and public relations consultant left suddenly over disagreements about how she should present her new image as the divorced wife of Britain's future king Prince Charles.
